title: `/login/totp` rejects backup-code logins for passkey-only MFA accounts
description: The `login_totp` handler guards on `not user.totp_enabled or not user.totp_secret` before calling `_consume_second_factor`. `POST /login` in `routes.py` issues an MFA ticket whenever `methods` is non-empty, which includes accounts with passkeys but no TOTP. A passkey-only account (totp_enabled=False, has passkeys) whose user tries `/login/totp` with a backup code always hits the 401 at line 264 (`not user.totp_enabled`). Backup codes are MFA-wide per the design (CLAUDE.md: 'Backup-Codes sind MFA-weit'), but the `/login/totp` gate contradicts this for the passkey-only case, making backup-code recovery impossible for those users.
recommendation: Remove the `not user.totp_enabled` / `not user.totp_secret` guard, or replace it with a check that the user has any MFA factor (totp_enabled OR passkey_count > 0). The `_consume_second_factor` helper already handles both TOTP and backup-code paths correctly; the outer guard is redundant and too narrow.

verdict.reasoning:
The bug is confirmed by reading the actual code. Three code paths together establish it:

1. `/login` in `routes.py` (lines 370-386): issues an MFA ticket whenever `passkey_count > 0`, even when `totp_enabled=False`. A passkey-only account gets `methods=["webauthn"]` and a valid `mfa_ticket`.

2. `/login/totp` in `routes_totp.py` (lines 260-269): the guard is `not user.totp_enabled or not user.totp_secret`. For a passkey-only account both conditions are true (`totp_enabled=False`, `totp_secret=None`), so the handler raises 401 and never reaches `_consume_second_factor`, regardless of what's in `payload.backup_code`.

3. `webauthn_register_verify` in `routes_webauthn.py` (lines 159-168): passkey-only accounts DO receive backup codes on first passkey registration (when `not has_codes`). The `_consume_second_factor` helper (lines 319-336) handles backup codes independently of `totp_enabled`/`totp_secret` — it only needs a matching `BackupCode` row. So the helper would work fine if only the outer guard were removed.

The impact path is entirely reachable: a user with only a passkey (no TOTP), who loses their authenticator device and tries to use their backup code via `POST /login/totp`, is permanently locked out. The `/login/totp` endpoint is the only backup-code consumption path for login; WebAuthn login (`/login/webauthn/*`) requires an actual credential that the user no longer has. The CLAUDE.md design intent states "Backup-Codes sind MFA-weit" (backup codes are MFA-wide), but the guard contradicts this for passkey-only accounts.

title: Profile-statement cache logic is inverted: cache is bypassed for fresh entries
description: The condition `if age >= _CACHE_STALE_SECS and age < _STATEMENT_TTL_SECS - 60: return {"token": token}` serves the cached token only when `age >= 5s`. When `age < 5s` (within the first 5 seconds after issue) the condition is false and `_issue_statement` is called, minting a new JWT and discarding the just-cached token. Every request within the first 5 seconds after any issue will produce a new token. The intended semantics (serve from cache until near-expiry, re-issue only when near expiry) are the opposite of what is implemented.
recommendation: Fix to serve the cache when the token is not near expiry: `if cached is not None and age < _STATEMENT_TTL_SECS - 60: return {"token": token}`. The 5-second `_CACHE_STALE_SECS` constant appears to be leftover or should be removed/re-evaluated.

verdict.reasoning: The logic at line 76 reads: `if age >= _CACHE_STALE_SECS and age < _STATEMENT_TTL_SECS - 60: return {"token": token}`. The lower bound `age >= 5.0` means the cache is bypassed for the first 5 seconds after any entry is stored. During that window every request falls through to `_issue_statement()`, which writes a fresh entry to `_STATEMENT_CACHE[user.id]` with a new `issued_at = int(time.time())`. This resets the clock, so the next request is again within the 5-second window and again bypasses the cache, creating a perpetual re-issuance loop as long as requests arrive more frequently than every 5 seconds. The intended semantics are clearly the opposite: serve from cache while the token is not near expiry (`age < _STATEMENT_TTL_SECS - 60`), and re-issue only when near expiry. The `_CACHE_STALE_SECS` constant creates an inverted guard that defeats the cache. No other code path compensates for this — `_invalidate_statement_cache` is only called on profile/username updates, not on every issue. The bug is exactly as described.

title: `DELETE /me` skips second-factor verification for passkey-only MFA accounts
description: The second-factor gate in `delete_me` checks only `if current.totp_enabled`. Accounts where MFA is passkey-only (`totp_enabled=False`, but with at least one `WebAuthnCredential`) skip it entirely. A stolen bearer token (valid up to 15 min) plus knowledge of the password can delete a passkey-only MFA account without any second-factor challenge. Account deletion is irreversible and hard-deletes the chat-side state.
recommendation: Extend the second-factor gate: check `totp_enabled OR passkey_count > 0`, mirroring the logic in `routes.py::login` where both conditions contribute to `methods`. For the passkey case, require a backup code (no interactive passkey challenge is feasible here).

verdict.reasoning:
The code at routes_account.py:134 reads `if current.totp_enabled:` — the second-factor block executes only when TOTP is on. For a passkey-only account (`totp_enabled=False`, ≥1 WebAuthnCredential row), this condition is false and the entire block is skipped; deletion proceeds after just password + confirm_username.

The login route (routes.py:364-386) explicitly checks BOTH conditions — `totp_enabled` AND `passkey_count > 0` — before issuing an MFA ticket, confirming the project's intent that passkey-only accounts are MFA-gated. The delete endpoint does not mirror this logic.

The fix infrastructure already exists: `AccountDeleteIn` already has a `backup_code` field, backup codes are issued to passkey-only accounts on first passkey registration (routes_totp.py:185-190 confirms codes persist when a passkey remains), and `_consume_second_factor` accepts backup codes without requiring `totp_secret`. The guard just needs to be `if current.totp_enabled or passkey_count > 0:` to close the gap.

title: MFA and challenge tickets decoded without `aud`/`iss` validation
description: `decode_mfa_ticket` calls `jwt.decode` with only `options={"require": ["exp", "sub"]}`, omitting the `audience` and `issuer` parameters. The same applies to `decode_challenge_ticket` in `passkeys.py:103-108`. A token signed by this service's private key but with a different `iss`/`aud` (e.g. issued by a staging environment sharing the same keypair, or crafted by any code path that signs without `iss`/`aud`) would pass signature verification. The `purpose` claim check is the only guard. `pyjwt` skips `iss`/`aud` validation silently when those parameters are absent from the `decode` call.
recommendation: Pass `issuer` and `audience` to `jwt.decode` in both `decode_mfa_ticket` (recovery.py) and `decode_challenge_ticket` (passkeys.py), matching the pattern in `JwtSigner.decode`.

verdict.reasoning:
The code confirms the technical finding exactly as described. In `recovery.py:100-104`, `decode_mfa_ticket` calls `jwt.decode` without `audience` or `issuer` parameters. In `passkeys.py:103-107`, `decode_challenge_ticket` does the same. The corresponding issuers (`issue_mfa_ticket` and `issue_challenge_ticket`) also deliberately omit `iss`/`aud` from the token payload — the comments in the source say so explicitly: "No `iss`/`aud` here — … we keep verification simple" and "deliberately skip the iss/aud claims."

The contrast with `JwtSigner.decode` (security.py:142-152) is clear: the main access/refresh token path passes both `audience=self._settings.jwt_audience` and `issuer=self._settings.jwt_issuer`, while these internal ticket decoders do not.

The `purpose` claim check (`payload.get("purpose") != "mfa"`) is the only guard, as the reviewer states. A token signed by the same RSA private key with `purpose=mfa` and a valid `sub`/`exp` would pass, regardless of what `iss`/`aud` it carries (or lacks).

The practical impact is limited: these tickets are consumed within the same auth-svc instance they are issued from (5-minute TTL, no cross-service boundary), so exploitation requires either key reuse across environments or an attacker who can already sign with the private key — in which case they have larger problems. However, the finding is real: if the same keypair is shared between a cloud and self-host instance (both use the same default `secrets/jwt_*.pem` in many self-host deployments), an MFA ticket issued on one instance would be accepted by the other. Adding `issuer`/`audience` to both the issuance and decode paths would close this gap at zero cost, matching the pattern already used by `JwtSigner.decode`. The severity is medium at most — not critical — but the issue is real and the fix is trivial.

title: N+1 DB queries in list_applications and list_instances (admin routes)
description: Both `GET /admin/instance-applications` and `GET /admin/instances` load rows with `session.execute(select(...))`, then loop over the results and call `await session.refresh(row, ["applicant"])` / `await session.refresh(row, ["registrar"])` once per row. Each `refresh` call issues a separate `SELECT` against the `users` table. For N applications/instances this produces N+1 round-trips to the database. The `applicant` and `registrar` relationships are already declared on the models, so a single query with `selectinload` or `joinedload` would eliminate the extra round-trips entirely.
recommendation: Add `.options(selectinload(InstanceApplication.applicant))` to the query in `list_applications` and `.options(selectinload(RegisteredInstance.registrar))` to the query in `list_instances`. Remove the per-row `await session.refresh(...)` calls. The relationship attributes will then be populated in one extra batched SELECT instead of N individual ones.

verdict.reasoning: The code at the referenced lines does exactly what the reviewer describes. In `list_applications` (lines 183-201), after the initial `select(InstanceApplication)` query, there is a per-row `await session.refresh(row, ["applicant"])` inside a loop — one extra SELECT against the `users` table for each application row. In `list_instances` (lines 344-360), the same pattern appears with `await session.refresh(row, ["registrar"])`. The relationship declarations in `models_instances.py` (lines 67 and 123) use plain `relationship(...)` with no `lazy="selectin"` or other eager-loading strategy, so no automatic batching occurs. The `session.refresh(row, attribute_list)` call in SQLAlchemy async always issues a fresh SELECT for the specified attributes — it does not batch across multiple objects. For N rows this produces exactly N+1 round-trips. The impact is limited by context (admin-only endpoint, cloud-gated via `_require_cloud`, low expected row counts), but the inefficiency is genuine and the recommended fix (`selectinload`) is correct.

title: Missing functional index for case-insensitive user search on username and display_name
description: `GET /users/search` builds the WHERE clause as `LOWER(username) LIKE 'prefix%'` and `LOWER(display_name) LIKE 'prefix%'`. There are no functional/expression indexes on `LOWER(username)` or `LOWER(display_name)` in `models.py` — only the plain `unique=True` B-tree on `username`. PostgreSQL cannot use a plain B-tree on `username` to satisfy `LOWER(username) LIKE 'prefix%'`; it falls back to a full sequential scan of the `users` table on every autocomplete keystroke. Even at a few thousand users this will be noticeably slow and grow linearly.
recommendation: Add two expression indexes in a migration: `CREATE INDEX ix_users_username_lower ON auth.users (LOWER(username) text_pattern_ops)` and `CREATE INDEX ix_users_display_name_lower ON auth.users (LOWER(display_name) text_pattern_ops)` (use `text_pattern_ops` so LIKE prefix matching can use the index). Mirror these in `User.__table_args__` using `Index('ix_users_username_lower', func.lower(User.username), postgresql_ops={'lower': 'text_pattern_ops'})`.

verdict.reasoning: The code at routes_search.py:76-77 does exactly what the reviewer claims: it applies `func.lower(User.username).like(pattern)` and `func.lower(User.display_name).like(pattern)` as WHERE conditions. The User model in models.py has no `__table_args__` at all — no functional/expression index on LOWER(username) or LOWER(display_name) exists anywhere. A grep across all 22 Alembic migrations and the model source finds zero instances of `username_lower`, `display_name_lower`, or `text_pattern_ops`. Only the plain unique B-tree on `username` (created in migration 0001_initial via `unique=True`) exists, which PostgreSQL cannot use to satisfy `LOWER(username) LIKE 'prefix%'`. Ironically the route's own docstring claims "Prefix-only (not full-text) keeps the query indexable" — but the required expression index was never created. The impact path is fully reachable: every autocomplete keystroke on the friends-add UI hits this sequential scan.

title: Uncached SmtpSettings DB hit on every /login and /me request
description: `_email_gate_blocked()` is called for every `_issue_tokens()` invocation (login, refresh, TOTP login, WebAuthn login, register) and also on every `GET /me`. Each call goes to `resolve_smtp_config(session)` which does `session.get(SmtpSettings, 1)` — a synchronous DB round-trip. The `SmtpSettings` singleton changes only when an admin explicitly updates it through the admin panel (a rare operation), but it is read on every authentication event. On a busy instance this is a gratuitous DB read on every hot-path request.
recommendation: Cache the `SmtpConfig` result in an in-process variable with a short TTL (e.g. 60 seconds), similar to the `_trusted_networks_cache` and `_STATEMENT_CACHE` patterns already in the codebase. Invalidate the cache whenever an admin updates SMTP settings via `routes_admin_smtp.py`. This converts the per-request DB query into a memory lookup on the critical login/refresh path.

verdict.reasoning: The code confirms the claim. `_email_gate_blocked()` (routes.py:65-76) has an early return only when `user.email_verified_at is not None` — for any unverified user it falls through to `resolve_smtp_config(session)` (email.py:104-109), which unconditionally calls `session.get(SmtpSettings, 1)` (email.py:67). Each request gets a fresh `AsyncSession` (db.py:45-47 via `get_session()`), so SQLAlchemy's per-session identity map provides no cross-request caching. There is no TTL cache or module-level variable guarding `SmtpSettings` reads anywhere in email.py or routes.py. The reviewer's comparison to `_trusted_networks_cache` (routes.py:595-618) and `_STATEMENT_CACHE` (routes_profile.py:27) is apt — those patterns exist but are not applied here. The DB hit fires on every call to `_issue_tokens` (login, refresh, TOTP-login, WebAuthn-login, register) and on every `GET /me` for any user whose `email_verified_at` is NULL. The severity is correctly assessed as medium: it is a real gratuitous DB query on hot paths, though its impact is bounded by the early-out for verified users and the fact that `session.get` by primary key is fast.

title: O(N) linear sweep of entire rate-bucket map on every rate-limited request
description: Every call to `_check_rate()` iterates over ALL entries in the per-endpoint `bucket` dict (`[k for k, w in bucket.items() if now - w["start"] >= seconds]`) to evict expired windows before checking the caller's slot. With multiple high-frequency endpoints (login: 20/min, user-search: 30/min) and many concurrent IPs, the bucket can grow large — each incoming request pays an O(N) scan over all currently-tracked IPs even when the caller's own window is still live. The identical pattern is repeated in `routes_credentials.py:46`. On a public-facing cloud instance under load this becomes a measurable CPU cost per request.
recommendation: Either (a) stop evicting proactively on every request and instead evict lazily only when the specific caller's key is a hit-and-miss (the common case does only two dict lookups), or (b) replace the per-endpoint dict with a structure that supports O(1) expiry (e.g. a `collections.OrderedDict` by insertion time). For production scale the comment in the code already acknowledges Redis should be used; a Redis-backed limiter eliminates this entirely.

verdict.reasoning: The code at routes.py:643-646 does exactly what the reviewer describes: `expired = [k for k, w in bucket.items() if now - w["start"] >= seconds]` performs a full linear scan over all IP entries in the per-endpoint bucket dict on every single call to `_check_rate`, before then doing the actual caller lookup. The identical pattern is confirmed at routes_credentials.py:46-48. The docstring's use of "lazily" is misleading — it describes when entries get dropped (after their window), not how the scan is done (it sweeps all N entries unconditionally). The reviewer's specific claim that this happens even when the caller's own window is still live (the common case) is confirmed: the eviction sweep at lines 643-646 happens before the per-caller check at line 648. The endpoints are public-facing (login at 20/min, user_search at 30/min), so under load or a credential-stuffing attack with many source IPs the bucket grows proportionally and each request pays an O(N) cost. The pattern is real and structurally identical in both files. Severity is medium rather than high because auth endpoints are not the hot path (chat/WS traffic dwarfs auth), and within a single time window the bucket size is bounded by the number of distinct active IPs — in practice likely hundreds to low thousands, not millions. Still a genuine performance defect worth fixing.

title: revoke_all_for_user loads all session rows into Python then updates one-by-one
description: `revoke_all_for_user()` issues a `SELECT` to load all active `UserSession` rows for a user into application memory, then sets `row.expires_at = now` in a Python loop, relying on SQLAlchemy's unit-of-work to flush N individual `UPDATE` statements. A user with many active sessions (browser + multiple devices) produces N round-trips. The same logic could be expressed as a single bulk `UPDATE ... WHERE user_id = ? AND expires_at > ?` that the DB executes atomically in one query. This is called on Logout-Everywhere, which is already a sensitive/performance-critical path.
recommendation: Replace the SELECT+loop with a single `await db.execute(update(UserSession).where(UserSession.user_id == user_id, UserSession.expires_at > now).values(expires_at=now))` and return `result.rowcount`. Mirrors the pattern already used for `RefreshToken` bulk-revoke in `routes.py:436-440`.

There is no session count cap or guard anywhere. The bulk-UPDATE pattern for RefreshToken is confirmed at routes.py:436-440 (`update(RefreshToken).where(...).values(...)`). Additionally, `purge_expired_sessions` in the same file (lines 122-131) already uses a single-query `sa_delete` to demonstrate the author knows this pattern. The only import from sqlalchemy in browser_sessions.py is `delete` and `select` — `update` is not imported, confirming no bulk-update path exists in this function. The claim is substantiated in every detail.

title: broadcast_update spawns one httpx.AsyncClient per instance instead of sharing a client
description: The `_notify` coroutine inside `broadcast_update` creates a fresh `httpx.AsyncClient(...)` for every instance it contacts, inside `asyncio.gather`. Each `AsyncClient` allocates its own connection pool and TLS context. With N active registered instances, this creates N independent TLS handshakes concurrently with no connection reuse. While this endpoint is rarely called, the resource overhead is unnecessary — a single shared client passed to all coroutines would reuse connections and share the TLS session cache.
recommendation: Instantiate one `httpx.AsyncClient` before the `asyncio.gather` call and pass it into each `_notify` coroutine as a parameter. Use `async with` at the outer scope and `async with asyncio.timeout(...)` per-call inside the coroutine for per-instance timeouts.

The inner `_notify` coroutine creates `async with httpx.AsyncClient(verify=True, timeout=5.0) as hx:` on line 277 — a brand-new client per instance — and all `_notify` calls run concurrently via `asyncio.gather` on line 288. There is no module-level or app-level shared httpx client anywhere in auth-svc (confirmed by grep across all files). Each concurrent call gets its own TLS context, its own connection pool, and performs its own TLS handshake to each instance hostname. The reviewer's description is accurate and the recommended fix (single outer `async with httpx.AsyncClient(...) as hx:` before `gather`, passed into `_notify`) is the standard httpx best-practice. Severity remains medium because this endpoint is a rarely-called internal admin operation guarded by INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET, and the instance count is expected to stay small — but the inefficiency is real and unnecessary.

title: DELETE /me skips second-factor check for passkey-only MFA users
description: The account self-deletion endpoint guards the second-factor step only with `if current.totp_enabled:`. A user who has registered WebAuthn/passkey credentials but has `totp_enabled=False` passes straight through with only a password check. Since passkeys constitute MFA on this account (they gate `/login` via the `methods` list in routes.py:372-386), the deletion endpoint should require the same proof of MFA possession. An attacker who knows the victim's password and holds a valid access token (15-minute window) or session cookie can permanently delete a passkey-protected account without ever touching the passkey.
recommendation: After the password check, also query `WebAuthnCredential` for the user and, when `passkey_count > 0 and not current.totp_enabled`, require a backup code or add a WebAuthn assertion step. Alternatively, unify the guard to mirror the login MFA-gate: require a second factor whenever `totp_enabled OR passkey_count > 0`.

verdict.reasoning: The code at routes_account.py:134 confirms the issue exactly as described. The deletion endpoint guards the second-factor step only with `if current.totp_enabled:` — there is no passkey/WebAuthn count query. Contrast with the login MFA gate at routes.py:372-378, which queries `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM webauthn_credentials WHERE user_id=?` and routes any passkey-only account through the MFA path. The `AccountDeleteIn` schema (schemas.py:471-490) has no WebAuthn assertion field, so even if the code tried to gate on passkeys it would have no credential to verify. The exploit is fully reachable: a 15-minute access token (jwt_access_ttl_seconds=900 in config.py) plus the victim's password is all that is needed to permanently delete a passkey-only MFA account, bypassing the second factor entirely.

title: TOTP codes are not invalidated after first use — replay within 90-second window
description: `pyotp.TOTP.verify(..., valid_window=1)` accepts any code from the previous, current, or next 30-second interval (up to 90 seconds total validity). The server never records a successfully consumed TOTP code. If an attacker can observe a valid TOTP code — for example, via a shoulder-surf, phishing page, or attacker-in-the-middle who relays it — they can replay it at `/login/totp` or `/totp/disable` within the same ~90-second window to pass MFA a second time. The 20/minute rate limit reduces exposure but does not prevent a replayed code arriving seconds after the legitimate use.
recommendation: Track the last accepted TOTP counter value per user (a single integer column on the User row or a short-lived Redis key). Reject any code whose counter is <= the last accepted counter. pyotp exposes the counter via `TOTP.timecode(datetime.now())` for comparison. Backup codes already have the correct `used_at` pattern to copy.

verdict.reasoning: The code confirms the vulnerability exactly as described. In `_consume_second_factor` (routes_totp.py line 318), TOTP verification is: `return pyotp.TOTP(user.totp_secret).verify(code, valid_window=1)`. With `valid_window=1`, pyotp accepts codes from the previous, current, and next 30-second interval — up to ~90 seconds of validity. There is no mechanism to record a consumed code: the `User` model has only `totp_secret` and `totp_enabled` columns, with no `totp_last_counter` or similar field. No Redis-based used-code set exists anywhere in the auth service (confirmed by grepping for "totp_counter", "totp_last", "totp_used", "replay" — nothing relevant). The MFA ticket JWT is also not marked consumed after its first use, though that is a separate issue. By contrast, backup codes correctly stamp `used_at` preventing replay. The rate limit of 20/minute does not prevent a replay attack that arrives seconds after the legitimate use. An attacker who observes a valid TOTP code (phishing, shoulder-surf, AITM) can replay it at `/login/totp`, `/totp/disable`, or `/totp/backup-codes/regenerate` within the ~90-second window to pass MFA a second time. The fix — storing the last accepted counter value and rejecting codes whose counter is ≤ the last accepted — is standard practice and straightforward to implement.

title: Non-constant-time comparison for INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET in broadcast_update
description: The `_require_internal_secret` helper and the inline check inside `broadcast_update` both compare the submitted bearer token with the configured secret using plain Python string `!=` (`token != secret`, lines 204 and 240). While exploiting this across an HTTP connection is difficult due to network jitter, the inconsistency is unnecessary given that `hmac.compare_digest` is already used elsewhere in the same codebase.

Line 204 in `_require_internal_secret` uses `if token != secret:` and line 240 inside `broadcast_update` duplicates the same plain `!=` comparison. There is no other guard or wrapper that closes the timing gap in routes_suspended_instances.py. The inconsistency is genuine and unnecessary — the fix pattern already exists in the codebase. Severity is low because exploiting a timing side-channel over an HTTP connection is very difficult due to network jitter, and the protected endpoint is internal-only, but the issue is real.

title: In-process rate limiter state is not shared across uvicorn workers
description: The rate-limiter (`_check_rate`) stores per-IP counters in `app.state.rate_buckets`, which is a plain Python dict living in the uvicorn worker process. With a single worker (the current production deployment) this is correct. The code's own comment acknowledges this: "Production deployments should swap to a Redis-backed limiter." If the operator ever scales to multiple workers (e.g., `uvicorn --workers 4` or a Gunicorn+uvicorn deployment), each process keeps an independent counter. An attacker can then multiply their allowed attempts by the number of workers. The login endpoint allows 20/minute per IP — with 4 workers that becomes 80/minute, substantially weakening brute-force protection.
recommendation: Replace the in-process bucket with a Redis-backed counter (e.g., `INCR` + `EXPIRE` or a sliding-window script). The Redis connection is already present in the service (`redis_url` config). Until then, document in the deployment guide that `--workers > 1` is unsafe with the current rate limiter.

verdict.reasoning:
The code at routes.py:621-657 confirms the claim exactly. `_check_rate` stores per-IP counters in `request.app.state.rate_buckets`, which is a plain Python dict initialized in app.py (`app.state.rate_buckets = {}`). The docstring explicitly acknowledges: "Production deployments should swap to a Redis-backed limiter." The login endpoint uses `settings.rate_limit_login` which defaults to "20/minute" (confirmed in config). No Redis-backed alternative exists — all rate limit paths (login, register, cert credential issuance in routes_credentials.py) use the same in-process dict.

However, the current production deployment is NOT presently vulnerable: `Dockerfile.service` line 66 starts uvicorn with `CMD exec uvicorn "${SVC_PKG}.app:app" --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000` — no `--workers` flag, so it runs a single worker. The risk is a latent configuration hazard: if an operator adds `--workers N` (e.g., to handle more load), the rate limit multiplies by N. title: assign_member_role does not validate target user membership before insert

title: Socket leaked in connection manager when ready-frame fails after register()

title: profile_statement handler closes WebSocket without breaking the op-loop

The simplest fix is to have the handler raise `WebSocketDisconnect` (or a custom `_WsCloseRequested` exception) which the caller catches alongside the normal disconnect. title: CRL revocation check fails open on Redis error, allowing revoked certs to authenticate
description: In `validate_cert`, the CRL membership check at line 173-176 catches all Redis exceptions and sets `is_revoked = False`. If Redis is unavailable (network partition, OOM kill, restart), every cert-login attempt silently bypasses the revocation check. An attacker holding a known-revoked Identity Cert can authenticate to any Self-Host instance whenever the CRL Redis key (`auth:revoked:certs`) is unreachable. The CLAUDE.md explicitly calls this out as a concern: 'Without this task the `auth:revoked:certs` Redis set stays empty in prod and revoked certs would pass validation (security hole)'. The current code extends this window to any transient Redis error, not just cold-cache startup.
recommendation: Distinguish between a cold cache (set is empty / key absent) and a Redis error. On a Redis error, return `None` from `validate_cert` (fail-closed) rather than treating it as 'not revoked'. If fail-open is explicitly desired for availability, document this as a policy decision, add a metric/alert for CRL-check failures, and consider caching the last-known-good CRL state in process memory so a brief Redis outage doesn't open the hole.

Combined with a valid signature (which can be verified from the JWKS already cached in process memory — though that path also has a Redis call, if the JWKS key is absent from Redis the JWKS lookup returns `{}` and the pub_key lookup fails, making sig_ok=False and returning None; however if the JWKS Redis key was populated before the outage, the JWKS cache path also fails open but sig_ok stays False since `await redis.get(cache_key)` in `_get_jwks_keys` would throw, returning `{}` — meaning actually a full Redis outage blocks auth entirely through the JWKS path too).

So a total Redis outage would cause `validate_cert` to raise at line 143 (`keys = await _get_jwks_keys(redis)`), not silently pass.

More importantly, the code makes an explicit architectural choice: JWKS fetch errors propagate (fail-closed by exception), but CRL lookup errors are caught and treated as "not revoked" (fail-open). title: Plugin pub/sub channels are not re-subscribed after listener crash recovery
description: The `start()` method only subscribes the five built-in channels (VOICE, GUILD, STREAM, WATCH, USER events). title: _filter_by_view_channel opens N concurrent DB sessions on cold cache, each running 3-5 queries

title: _filter_presence_visibility is O(N_targets × N_all_sockets)
description: On every `presence_update` or `presence_status_changed` guild event, `_filter_presence_for_sender` (pubsub_channel_guild.py:26-51) calls `_filter_presence_visibility(target_user_ids, sender_uid)`. The inner loop iterates the full `_ws_user` dict for every entry in `target_user_ids` (line 201: `for ws, u in self._ws_user.items()`). With C connected sockets and T targets (worst case T = all connected users minus sender), this is O(T × C). At 500 connected sockets where 400 are unique users, a single presence event fires 400 outer iterations × 500 inner iterations = 200,000 dict lookups per event. The `_GUILD_MEMBER_SCOPED_OPS` pre-filter reduces T for member-scoped events, but `presence_update` and `presence_status_changed` deliberately skip that filter (pubsub_channel_guild.py:88, 101) and operate on all connections.
recommendation: Maintain a reverse index `_user_sockets: dict[int, set[WebSocket]]` (the existing `_user_conns` serves this role) and rewrite the inner loop to look up `_user_conns.get(uid)` directly instead of scanning all sockets. This reduces the complexity to O(T + total_sockets_for_target_users).

verdict.reasoning: The code at pubsub_friend_cache.py:199-213 confirms the bug exactly. `_filter_presence_visibility` loops over `target_user_ids` and for each uid scans the entire `_ws_user` dict (`for ws, u in self._ws_user.items(): if u.id != uid: continue`), making it O(T × C). The reverse index `_user_conns: dict[int, set[WebSocket]]` already exists in pubsub.py line 83 and is used correctly in the similar `is_blocked_by_any_socket` method (lines 61-71) via `self._user_conns.get(target_user_id)` — but `_filter_presence_visibility` does not use it. Both `presence_update` (pubsub_channel_guild.py:88) and `presence_status_changed` (line 101) explicitly call `_filter_presence_for_sender` which feeds all connected sockets as `target_uids`, not a guild-scoped subset, confirming the worst-case path. The fix is straightforward: replace the inner scan with `_user_conns.get(uid)` as already done in `is_blocked_by_any_socket`.

title: _load_context fires a separate SELECT for the @everyone role after fetching assigned roles
description: `_load_context` first fetches the member's assigned roles via a JOIN query (line 113-120), then issues a second separate SELECT to fetch the @everyone role (lines 123-126), checks if it's already in the result set (Python list `__contains__`, O(n)), and conditionally appends. This means every `resolve_permissions` call where the user is a member (which is the normal case — it is called in subscribe, send, profile_statement, admin checks, and for every socket during cold-cache broadcast filtering) pays 2 role-related round-trips instead of 1. The second query is cheap (partial index on `is_everyone`), but at 100+ concurrent cold-cache `_filter_by_view_channel` calls, 100 extra round-trips add up. Additionally the `everyone not in assigned` check is a linear scan of the assigned list.
recommendation: Merge both fetches into one query with `OR` (e.g. `WHERE (member_roles join) OR is_everyone`) or simply always include the @everyone role by filtering `roles_by_guild` with `is_everyone=True` from the already-loaded role list in the caller, as the ready-frame's `resolve_guild_permissions_from_snapshot` already does.

verdict.reasoning: The code at `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/permissions.py` lines 111-137 does exactly what the reviewer describes. When the user is a member, `_load_context` first executes a JOIN query fetching roles from `member_roles` (lines 112-120), then unconditionally executes a second SELECT for the `@everyone` role (lines 123-126), and checks `if everyone is not None and everyone not in assigned` (line 127) — the latter being a Python list `__contains__` scan. Since `@everyone` is implicit and never stored in `member_roles`, it will never appear in the first JOIN query result, so the second SELECT is effectively always executed and always appended — the guard condition is vacuously always true in practice. The O(n) list scan is real but harmless (role count per member is tiny). The hot-path impact is confirmed: `pubsub_perm_filter.py`'s `_filter_by_view_channel` (line 261-305) calls `asyncio.gather` over all connected sockets and each cold-cache resolution goes through `resolve_permissions` → `_load_context`. The comment at lines 300-301 in `pubsub_perm_filter.py` explicitly acknowledges "Sequential awaits here scale linearly with target count (100 voice-presence subscribers → 100 round-trips on a cold cache)", indirectly confirming the per-socket double-query overhead. The caching layer (`_ws_perms` in `_resolve_channel_perms`) only helps on warm cache; on cold cache (e.g. after server restart, after invalidation, or first connect), every socket pays the two-round-trip cost. The fix of either merging into a single OR query or using `is_everyone=True` filtering from an already-loaded role list (as `resolve_guild_permissions_from_snapshot` does) is valid. Severity is medium as stated: it is a genuine inefficiency on cold-cache fan-out paths, not a correctness or security issue.

title: remove_socket iterates all channel subscriptions to find and clean up a single socket
description: `remove_socket` loops over every entry in `_subs` (all currently active channel subscriptions) to discard the departing socket. With many channels active across the instance (e.g. 50 guilds × 10 channels = 500 `_subs` entries), every disconnect scans all 500 entries. This runs inside the `_lock`, blocking other coroutines that need the lock (register, subscribe, unsubscribe, fan-out targets snapshot). Under high churn (mobile clients dropping frequently) this becomes a notable source of lock contention. The lock is an asyncio.Lock so it yields between holders, but the O(C_subscribed) work inside the critical section is still wasted.
recommendation: Maintain a per-socket reverse index `_ws_channels: dict[WebSocket, set[str]]` populated in `subscribe`/`unsubscribe`. Then `remove_socket` iterates only the channels that socket was subscribed to (typically 1-3) instead of all active channels.

verdict.reasoning: Lines 231-234 of /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/pubsub.py confirm the exact pattern described: `for cid in list(self._subs): self._subs[cid].discard(ws); if not self._subs[cid]: del self._subs[cid]`. This iterates the entire `_subs` dict (one entry per active channel subscription across all guilds and users on this instance) to find which channels held the departing socket. No `_ws_channels` reverse index exists anywhere in the codebase (grep confirmed zero hits). The `subscribe` method (line 206-207) only writes to the forward map `_subs[channel_id].add(ws)` — it never records which channels a given socket has joined. The `unsubscribe` method similarly only updates the forward map. The O(C_subscribed) scan runs inside `async with self._lock` (line 219), which is an `asyncio.Lock`, so every concurrent `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `register`, or fan-out snapshot call that needs the lock must wait for the full loop to complete. The reviewer's characterisation is accurate: the fix would be a reverse index `_ws_channels: dict[WebSocket, set[str]]` maintained in `subscribe`/`unsubscribe`, making `remove_socket` iterate only channels that socket actually joined (typically a handful) rather than all active channels across the instance.

title: fan_out_mention_events publishes one Redis message per mentioned user sequentially
description: After filtering, `fan_out_mention_events` publishes a `mention_added` envelope to `user:events` channel with `await mgr.publish_user_event(uid, envelope)` inside a plain for-loop. Each `publish_user_event` is an individual `redis.publish` call. For a @everyone mention on a 100-member guild this is 100 sequential awaits, each a round-trip to Redis. While the Redis round-trip is fast (~0.5ms), 100 sequential calls = ~50ms of wall-clock time holding up the send handler (the comment at line 351 wraps it in try/except but still awaits sequentially).
recommendation: Gather the publishes concurrently with `asyncio.gather(*(mgr.publish_user_event(uid, envelope) for uid in filtered), return_exceptions=True)` to keep total latency bounded by one Redis round-trip instead of N.

verdict.reasoning: The code at `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/mentions.py` lines 348-352 does exactly what the reviewer describes: a plain `for uid in filtered:` loop with `await mgr.publish_user_event(uid, envelope)` inside each iteration. Each call goes to `pubsub.py:276-296` which does a single `await self._redis.publish(USER_EVENTS_CHANNEL, ...)` — one Redis round-trip per user. For a 100-member @everyone mention this is 100 sequential awaits. There is no existing batch path, pipeline, or `asyncio.gather` guard in this function. The rest of the codebase already uses `asyncio.gather` for fan-out patterns (pubsub.py lines 348 and 499), so the pattern is established. The finding is real and the recommended fix (`asyncio.gather`) is appropriate. The impact is low/moderate: Redis round-trips are fast (~0.5ms each), so 100 members = ~50ms of added latency in the send handler, which is non-trivial but not catastrophic.

title: Challenge token is not invalidated after single use — replay within TTL window is possible
description: The cert-login flow is stateless: a valid `challenge_token` + `signature` pair can be replayed up to the 60-second expiry window to obtain multiple session tokens without re-performing the Ed25519 signing step. The comment on line 30-32 acknowledges this is a 'known' window but mischaracterises the risk as only being about 'replaying the verify call', which is exactly what an attacker who intercepts the HTTPS response can do. In a self-host scenario where TLS termination is at a shared Caddy instance or the network path is otherwise attackable, the intercepted verify request body (cert + challenge_token + signature) can be replayed to `POST /cert-login/verify` within the TTL and produce a fresh 5-minute session token. Mitigation would be a Redis `SET NX EX 60` on the challenge token value to mark it consumed after first use.
recommendation: After a successful `verify`, mark the challenge token as consumed in Redis (`SET cert-login:used:<hash_of_challenge_token> 1 EX 60`). At the start of `cert_login_verify`, check the key's existence and reject with 410 if already used. This closes the replay window without adding per-state storage for the challenge phase itself.

verdict.reasoning: The code in cert_login.py confirms the vulnerability exactly as described. The `cert_login_verify` handler (lines 214-279) performs cert validation, HMAC challenge-token verification, cert_id cross-binding, and Ed25519 signature verification — but never marks the challenge token as consumed. There is no Redis SET NX, no used-token set, and no rate-limiting applied to either cert-login endpoint (ratelimit.py has no rule for cert_login, and the route never calls check()). The docstring comment (lines 30-32) explicitly acknowledges the 60-second replay window but dismisses it with "rate-limited by cert expiry + Ed25519 single-use semantics in the calling client" — those are client-side properties that do not prevent a network attacker who has already captured the completed {cert, challenge_token, signature} triple from replaying it directly to /cert-login/verify multiple times within the TTL window. The store_session_token call writes a fresh session token to Redis on each successful verify call, meaning each replay produces a distinct valid 5-minute session token. No other guard in the codebase (middleware, app.py, routes/__init__.py) closes this gap.

title: CRL lookup fails open on Redis error — revoked certs accepted during Redis outages
description: In `validate_cert`, the CRL Redis `sismember` call is wrapped in a bare `except Exception` that sets `is_revoked = False` on any error (line 176: 'fail-open on Redis error (same as previous good state)'). During a Redis outage or transient connection failure, a certificate that has been revoked (e.g., because the Cloud detected device compromise) will be accepted, and a session token will be issued. Since the cert-login flow (and subsequent WS auth via session tokens) provides the primary authentication path for self-hosted instances, this allows a holder of a revoked credential to authenticate for the duration of the Redis unavailability. The comment 'same as previous good state' is inaccurate — it conflates 'CRL was not updated' with 'CRL says not revoked'.
recommendation: Change the Redis error path to fail-closed: if the CRL lookup throws, set `is_revoked = True` (or equivalently, return `None` from `validate_cert`). Alternatively, log a critical-severity event and refuse authentication until Redis recovers. The 30-second CRL poll interval means the in-Redis set is at most 30 seconds stale during normal operation, so using a stale but present set is safe; but when the set is unreachable the correct default is to deny.

verdict.reasoning:
The code at /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/credential_validator.py lines 173-176 does exactly what the reviewer describes. The `sismember` call for CRL lookup is wrapped in a bare `except Exception` that sets `is_revoked = False`, allowing a revoked cert to pass validation if Redis throws any error.

The reviewer's claim about the comment being inaccurate is also correct: "fail-open on Redis error (same as previous good state)" conflates two distinct states — (a) Redis is reachable and the set says the cert is not revoked, vs. (b) Redis is unreachable and we cannot determine revocation status. Only (a) is a "good state"; (b) is an unknown state that the code treats as safe.

One important nuance worth noting: a complete Redis outage would also cause `_get_jwks_keys` (line 86: `await redis.get(cache_key)`) to fail. That function catches exceptions by returning an empty dict (lines 93-94), which leads to `pub_key = None` → `sig_ok = False` → the function returns `None` (rejection). So a total Redis outage would actually fail-closed for cert validation as a whole, since the JWKS lookup would also fail.

However, the fail-open CRL path is still a real vulnerability in partial failure scenarios — for example:
- Redis connection is up but the specific `sismember` command times out or returns an error (e.g., READONLY error during failover, WRONGTYPE error, memory limit hit for commands affecting sets but not gets)
- The JWKS key is still readable (warm `GET`), but the revoked-certs set operation fails
- Race condition during Redis restart where the JWKS key has been restored but the revoked set hasn't yet been repopulated

In such scenarios, the JWKS `GET` succeeds (returning cached keys), signature verification passes, but the CRL `sismember` throws and `is_revoked` is silently set to `False`, allowing a revoked cert through.

The fix is straightforward: on CRL lookup exception, either set `is_revoked = True` (fail-closed) or re-raise and let `validate_cert` return `None`. The reviewer's recommendation is sound.

title: `/internal/jwks-status` endpoint is publicly reachable through nginx proxy
description: The endpoint `GET /internal/jwks-status` is registered directly on the FastAPI app (not behind any auth middleware). It returns `jwks_ready` and `jwks_changed_unexpectedly` flags. The nginx config (`infra/prod/web-nginx.conf`) proxies the entire `/api/chat/` prefix to the chat-gateway, which means a request to `https://howispulse.com/api/chat/internal/jwks-status` will reach this endpoint unauthenticated. The code comment says 'not exposed publicly — the nginx / Caddy layer should restrict this to localhost / internal networks', but there is no such restriction in the nginx config: there is no `deny all` block, no IP allowlist, and no `/internal/` negation location. While the information disclosed (JWKS pin status) is low-sensitivity, the pattern violates the stated access model and could be extended by future additions.
recommendation: Add a `location /internal/ { deny all; }` block (placed before the `/api/chat/` proxy block) in `web-nginx.conf`, or add an auth dependency (e.g., `require_admin`) to all `/internal/` routes in the FastAPI app itself. The pattern used for `/internal/health-probe` (secret header gate) should be applied to `/internal/jwks-status` as well.

verdict.reasoning: The code confirms the claim. At `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/app.py:238`, the `/internal/jwks-status` GET endpoint is registered on the FastAPI app with no authentication dependency — it just reads two `app.state` flags and returns them. The nginx config at `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/infra/prod/web-nginx.conf` has a blanket `location /api/chat/` block that rewrites and proxies everything under that prefix (including `internal/jwks-status`) to the chat-gateway container, with no `/internal/` deny block or IP restriction anywhere in the file. The contrast with `/internal/health-probe` is real: that route (in `routes/health.py:158`) uses a `_check_internal_secret` call that validates an `X-Pulse-Internal-Secret` header. The code comment on `jwks-status` itself acknowledges the gap ("Not exposed publicly — the nginx / Caddy layer should restrict this to localhost / internal networks") but no such restriction exists. The information disclosed (two booleans about JWKS pin state) is low-sensitivity but the pattern violation and inconsistency with the stated access model are genuine. Severity is low rather than medium because the disclosed data is two boolean health flags with no authentication material, not credentials or PII.

title: In-process rate limiter is per-pod and easily bypassed in multi-instance deployments
description: The rate-limit buckets are stored in a module-level dict that is local to each chat-gateway process. With Watchtower rolling updates or if the service were scaled horizontally, each pod starts with an empty bucket. A client that opens connections to different pods (which is possible through the nginx upstream round-robin once old pod is replaced) can send N×limit messages per second where N = number of pods. For the current single-pod deployment this is a non-issue, but the code comment itself flags it as an unresolved TODO ('for a multi-instance deployment behind Caddy this must be swapped for a Redis-backed limiter'). The current limit of 10 messages/second per user means a single-pod attacker can only send 600 messages/minute, which is reasonable but not formally enforced at infra level.
recommendation: Move rate-limit state to Redis (e.g., using a Lua sliding-window script or `redis-py-rate-limit`) before scaling beyond one pod. As a stopgap for the current single-pod deployment, the existing behaviour is acceptable but should be documented as a deployment constraint.

verdict.reasoning: The claim is accurate and well-supported by the code. The rate-limit state in `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/ratelimit.py` is held entirely in a module-level dict `_buckets` (line 16), using `time.monotonic()` which is also process-local. There is no Redis integration anywhere in this module. The file's own docstring at line 4-6 explicitly flags this: "It is *per process* — for a multi-instance deployment behind Caddy this must be swapped for a Redis-backed limiter." The production docker-compose (`infra/prod/docker-compose.yml`) uses `container_name: pulse_chat_gateway` with a single container and the Dockerfile (`Dockerfile.service` line 66) starts uvicorn with a single worker and no `--workers` flag, confirming single-pod deployment today. The issue is real but its severity is currently low because the deployment is provably single-pod and single-worker. The reviewer's characterisation of N×limit bypass being possible if scaled horizontally is technically correct, and the TODO in the code acknowledges it. There is no compensating control (no Redis-backed limiter, no infra-level rate limiting via Caddy/nginx) that would make this a non-issue.

title: Oversize-frame counter decrement allows indefinite abuse with alternating frame sizes
description: The `oversize_frames` counter decrements by 1 for every normal-sized frame (line 94: `oversize_frames = max(0, oversize_frames - 1)`). With `_MAX_OVERSIZE_FRAMES = 5`, an attacker can send 4 oversized frames (counter = 4), then 4 normal frames (counter = 0), then 4 oversized frames again, indefinitely, without ever reaching the disconnect threshold of 5. The intended behaviour was likely a sliding penalty window, but the implementation allows unbounded abuse as long as the pattern of 4 over / 4 under is maintained. This is a minor DoS vector: a single client can hold a socket open indefinitely while generating error-response processing on the server for each oversized frame.
recommendation: Change the semantics to a strict counter that only resets to 0 on disconnect, or use a true sliding window where the counter decays more slowly (e.g., only after N consecutive clean frames rather than 1). Alternatively, apply a backoff on error responses for oversized frames to add cost for the abuser.

verdict.reasoning: The code at /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/routes/ws_ops.py confirms the reviewer's claim exactly. Line 94 `oversize_frames = max(0, oversize_frames - 1)` decrements the counter by 1 for every normal-sized frame that passes the size check. With `_MAX_OVERSIZE_FRAMES = 5` (line 41), the disconnect only triggers at `oversize_frames >= 5` (line 91). An attacker can send 4 oversized frames (counter reaches 4, still below threshold), then send 4 normal frames (counter decrements back to 0), and repeat this pattern indefinitely. Each oversized frame causes the server to send an error response (lines 88-90: `send_json({"op": "error", "code": 4009, "msg": "frame too large"})`), meaning the server does real work per oversized frame. There is no other guard elsewhere in the function or file that would catch this alternating pattern. The exploit path is directly reachable by any authenticated WebSocket client.

title: `_apply_leave` splits presence-set and streaming-set cleanup into two separate `await redis.eval` calls, creating a window for inconsistent published snapshots
description: `_apply_leave` removes a user from the presence set (first `redis.eval`) and then from the streaming set (second `redis.eval`). These are two separate `await` points, so the asyncio event loop can schedule another coroutine between them. If a concurrent `participant_joined` (or any other event) for the same room arrives between the two evals, its `_publish_state` call will read a state where the leaving user is absent from `voice:room:channel-<id>` but still present in `voice:room:channel-<id>:streaming`. The resulting snapshot published on `voice:events` has `streaming_user_ids` containing a user who is not in `user_ids`, which is an invalid state that chat-gateway will fan out to all subscribed clients. Clients that respect `streaming_user_ids` exclusively (e.g. the screen-share badge in VoiceChannelView) will show a phantom streaming badge for the departed user until the next corrective snapshot.
recommendation:
Merge both SREM operations into a single Lua script that atomically removes `user_id` from both the presence set and the streaming set (and conditionally deletes each key when it becomes empty). This eliminates the inter-eval window entirely. Example sketch:

```lua
redis.call('SREM', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
if redis.call('SCARD', KEYS[1]) == 0 then redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end
redis.call('SREM', KEYS[2], ARGV[1])
if redis.call('SCARD', KEYS[2]) == 0 then redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2]) end
```
Call as `redis.eval(LUA, 2, room_key, streaming_key, user_id)`.

verdict.reasoning:
The code at lines 180-181 of /home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/voice-signaling/src/dcc_voice_signaling/webhook.py confirms the claim exactly. `_apply_leave` issues two separate `await redis.eval(...)` calls — one to remove the user from the presence set (`voice:room:channel-<id>`) and a second to remove them from the streaming set (`voice:room:channel-<id>:streaming`). There is an asyncio yield point between them.

FastAPI/uvicorn serves multiple concurrent requests in the same event loop with no per-room lock or serialization. A concurrent webhook request for the same room (e.g. a `track_published`/`participant_joined` for another user, or even a delayed duplicate event) that arrives between the two evals will reach `_publish_state`, which reads both sets in a non-transactional pipeline (line 145: `transaction=False`). At that moment the presence set already has the leaving user removed, but the streaming set still contains them, producing an invalid snapshot where `streaming_user_ids` contains a uid absent from `user_ids`. That snapshot is published on `voice:events` and chat-gateway fans it out to all connected clients.

The existing Lua scripts each make one key's operation atomic (SREM + conditional DEL), which the code comment at lines 177-179 explicitly acknowledges — but that atomicity is only within a single key. No guard exists between the two evals. There is no asyncio.Lock, semaphore, or per-room queue anywhere in the service (confirmed by searching all Python files). The fix described (merging both SREMs into a single two-key Lua script) would close the window entirely.

title: `_is_screen_share` track-name fallback fires unconditionally for any source, not only for source=UNKNOWN

If LiveKit ever sends a camera track with `name="screenshare"` (e.g., from a third-party client or a future LiveKit version), `_is_screen_share` returns True, causing that user to be added to the streaming set and broadcast as screen-sharing. title: `voice_override` and `voice_disconnect` endpoint path params `user_id`/`channel_id` have no format validation
description: The `PUT /channels/{channel_id}/members/{user_id}/voice-override` and `POST /channels/{channel_id}/members/{user_id}/voice-disconnect` route handlers declare `channel_id` and `user_id` as plain `str` with no length limit or pattern constraint. In contrast, the service-to-service `InternalEvictIn` model (internal.py:26) validates `user_id` with `pattern=r'^\d+$'` and `max_length=64`. An authenticated admin with `MUTE_MEMBERS` could craft a request with an arbitrarily long or non-numeric `user_id` (e.g. containing colons or newlines). This writes a malformed Redis key (`voice:override:channel-<cid>:user-<arbitrary>`) that persists for up to 24 hours and could cause a key-space collision or unexpected behaviour if a valid user ID later shares the same suffix. The `_livekit_update_participant` call would also construct an identity string `user-<arbitrary>` and silently fail when LiveKit rejects or ignores the malformed identity.
recommendation:
Add path-param validation matching `InternalEvictIn`:
```python
from fastapi import Path

channel_id: Annotated[str, Path(min_length=1, max_length=64, pattern=r'^\d+$')]
user_id: Annotated[str, Path(min_length=1, max_length=64, pattern=r'^\d+$')]
```
Apply the same fix to `voice_disconnect.py`.

verdict.reasoning:
The code confirms the claim exactly. In voice_override.py:34-35 and voice_disconnect.py:19-20, both `channel_id` and `user_id` are declared as plain `str` with no length limit or pattern constraint. In contrast, `InternalEvictIn` in internal.py:26 applies `pattern=r'^\d+$'` and `max_length=64` on `user_id`.

The unvalidated strings flow directly into `_override_key(channel_id, user_id)` → `f"voice:override:channel-{channel_id}:user-{user_id}"` (overrides_state.py:28) where they are persisted in Redis with a 24h TTL. They also flow into `_livekit_remove_participant`/`_livekit_update_participant` which constructs `identity=f"user-{user_id}"` (livekit_client.py:60, 102).

title: TOCTOU race in single-use publish-token deletion allows replay within the race window

The practical exploit path: an attacker who obtains the push URL (token in RTMPS password) and connects before or simultaneously with the real GSR client can have MediaMTX accept their connection first, hijacking the stream path while the real client gets rejected at the media layer. The nonce-per-session design means the hijacker occupies exactly the right path. Requires either TLS interception or a log/memory leak of the push URL to obtain the token.

The practical impact is moderate: exploiting it requires obtaining the token value (from TLS interception or a memory/log leak of the RTMPS push URL), and the race window between the GET and DELETE is very narrow (sub-millisecond in normal operation). However, a deliberate attacker who already has the token and fires two simultaneous connections to MediaMTX would reliably trigger this, since MediaMTX makes two near-simultaneous authHTTP calls for the two RTMPS connections. title: MediaMTX `{"items": null}` response causes TypeError and skips one entire reconciliation cycle

The consequence is that the entire self-heal reconciliation (including the `known - publishers` cleanup path) is skipped for that tick. title: `apply_atomic_update` uses two separate transactions, not one; unhandled `NoResultFound` between them can crash the handler

ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` followed immediately by `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in the same transaction is safe and standard. For the `scalar_one()` call, add a fallback (e.g., `scalar_one_or_none()` with a guard) to handle the rare concurrent-deletion case without crashing.

title: Async deactivate hooks are silently ignored (never awaited)

title: _broadcast_state_update iterates all connected WebSockets to find guild members (O(total_connections))
description: The channel handler acquires `manager._lock`, copies all `manager._connections` into a local list, then scans the entire list to find sockets whose `_ws_guilds` contains the target guild_id. With N total connected users across all guilds, this is O(N) per tamagotchi event. On a busy instance with many guilds/users the vast majority of the list is irrelevant to any single guild broadcast. Populate/remove on `register`/`remove_socket`/guild-join/guild-leave events. The broadcast path then becomes an O(1) lookup + O(guild_members) send instead of O(total_connections) scan. Under heavy feed-spam the event loop would be repeatedly iterating all connected sockets across all guilds, which is the actual performance concern regardless of lock granularity. The suggested fix (reverse guild→sockets index) is the standard remedy and does not exist today.

title: Two filesystem scans of the plugins/ directory on every admin PUT /admin/plugins/{name}
description: The PUT handler calls `discover_manifests()` (line 184) to validate the plugin exists, which runs `_parse_manifests_in_dir` — a full directory walk + TOML parse of every plugin. It then calls `activate_plugin(name)` (line 192), which, if the plugin is not already in the PluginManager, calls `_parse_manifests_in_dir` again (loader.py line 385). The first scan results are discarded. On a system with many plugins or slow storage (network filesystem, container overlay) this doubles the I/O cost of every admin activation. The hot-path case where the plugin was discovered at startup avoids the second scan, but the cold path (plugin dropped after service start) hits both.

1. `admin_plugins.py` line 184 always calls `discover_manifests()` → `_parse_manifests_in_dir()`: full directory walk + TOML parse of every plugin, just to check if `name` is present. This result is discarded (only a set of names is kept).

2. `activate_plugin()` at line 192 first checks `mgr.get(plugin_name)`. If the PluginManager already has the plugin record it returns immediately with no second scan.

The critical point: `load_directory_with_allowlist()` (the lifespan startup path) calls `mgr.add(manifest, directory)` for ALL discovered plugins — including ones NOT in the allowlist — so that they're visible to the admin API. This means any plugin present on disk at startup is in the PluginManager, making `mgr.get()` return non-None for any typical admin-activation scenario (plugin was already on disk, just not allowed).

So the second scan in `activate_plugin` only fires when a plugin directory was physically absent at service startup and was hot-dropped afterward. This is genuinely rare.

However, the FIRST scan (the `discover_manifests()` call for existence-checking) is redundant in ALL cases. The PluginManager already holds the full set of at-startup-discovered plugins. The PUT handler could simply check `mgr.get(name)` (or look at the manager's known set) instead of scanning the filesystem again. The first scan hits every admin PUT unconditionally, and its result (the set of names) is thrown away immediately after the 404 guard. That is a real I/O waste on every admin activation, even in the normal case.

The severity is low in practice: typical deployments have a handful of plugins (the repo has `hello` and `tamagotchi`), the directory walk is fast on local filesystems, and the endpoint is an infrequent admin operation. On network/overlay filesystems the cost matters more. The reviewer's framing of "doubles the I/O cost" is accurate only for the rare cold path; for the normal path it's one full scan plus a dict lookup. The issue is real but the practical impact is minor.

title: ws_op_gate per-plugin cache eviction is O(_MAX_ENTRIES) list-copy on each cache miss when full
description: `_cache_put` (line 111) checks `len(_cache) >= _MAX_ENTRIES` and, if full, calls `next(iter(_cache))` to pop the first dict key. Python 3.7+ dicts preserve insertion order, so this evicts the *oldest* inserted entry — even if it was inserted one second ago and is still hot — while a never-queried entry inserted three seconds earlier stays. This is FIFO, not LRU. With 4096 entries and 60-second TTL the worst-case behaviour is: a guild that feeds its tamagotchi every second fills the cache with recent (guild, plugin) entries; after 4096 entries an unrelated guild's entry at slot 0 gets evicted even though it was just written. The more important issue is that `_cache_put` creates a `list(_cache)` snapshot every time the cache is full (line 117: `next(iter(_cache))` actually does not copy, but the surrounding comment implies a future change risk). At `_MAX_ENTRIES=4096` this is negligible for the current plugin count, but scales linearly with entries.

However, the reviewer's central performance claim — that `_cache_put` does an O(N) `list(_cache)` copy on every eviction — is factually wrong. The actual code uses `next(iter(_cache))`, which is O(1) dict iteration, not a list copy. The real issue is purely FIFO semantics, not O(N) behaviour. The severity is also overstated: the code comment explicitly acknowledges this as a deliberate "naive eviction" trade-off for PR1, the TTL is 60 s, the cap is 4096 entries, and currently only one real plugin (`tamagotchi`) is deployed, making it practically impossible to fill the cache with 4096 distinct (guild_id, plugin_name) pairs within a 60-second window. The issue is real-but-theoretical at current scale, exactly as the code's own comment says.

title: Plugin entrypoint backend field allows path traversal outside plugin directory
description:
In `_load_plugin_module`, the entrypoint module name is taken directly from `plugin.toml`'s `backend` field (parsed via `ep.partition(':')`), which has no pattern constraint in the `PluginEntrypoints` model (`manifest.py:78`). The file path is constructed as `directory / f"{module_name}.py"` with no check that the resolved path stays within the plugin's own directory. A `plugin.toml` with `backend = "../../services/auth/src/dcc_auth/app:evil"` would cause `spec_from_file_location` to load and `exec_module` to execute an arbitrary `.py` file anywhere on the filesystem accessible to the process.

The attack requires: (1) ability to write a `plugin.toml` with a traversal path into the plugins directory on the server, AND (2) the Bootstrap-Admin to approve the plugin via `PUT /admin/plugins/{name}`. Because an admin who can write to the plugins directory already has server shell access, this does not represent a new principal boundary breach — but it silently elevates "write a TOML file" into "execute code outside the declared sandbox" through the admin UI, which is an unexpected and undocumented escalation path within the admin trust boundary.
recommendation: In `_load_plugin_module`, resolve `file_path` and verify it is inside `directory.resolve()` before proceeding: `if not file_path.resolve().is_relative_to(directory.resolve()): raise ValueError(...)`. Additionally, add a regex constraint to the `PluginEntrypoints.backend` field in `manifest.py` (e.g. `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*:register$`) so the TOML parser rejects traversal strings before the loader ever sees them.

In `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/plugins/registry.py` line 131, `module_name` is extracted as `ep.partition(':')[0]` from the raw `backend` string. At line 366 it is concatenated with `directory` using Python's `/` operator: `file_path = directory / f"{module_name}.py"`. Python's `Path.__truediv__` does NOT sanitize `..` components — a value like `../../services/auth/src/dcc_auth/app` produces a path that resolves entirely outside the plugin directory. There is no `is_relative_to` check, no `resolve()` containment guard, and no regex constraint on the `PluginEntrypoints.backend` field (manifest.py line 78 declares it as plain `str | None = None`). The `PluginName` type does have a pattern (`^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{1,31}$`) but that protects the plugin name, not the entrypoint path. Python test confirms the traversal resolves correctly.

The practical impact is limited: exploitation requires both filesystem write access to the plugins directory AND Bootstrap-Admin UI approval — as the reviewer notes, filesystem write access already implies server shell access, so no new principal boundary is crossed. This downgrades severity from high to medium. The defect is nonetheless real: it silently converts "write a TOML file" into "execute any .py file the server process can read" through a seemingly safe admin UI action, which is an undocumented escalation within the admin trust boundary.

title: Plugin can silently override core WS ops (e.g. 'send') bypassing the plugin gate entirely
description:
The plugin gate is only invoked when `parse_plugin_op(op) is not None`, i.e. when the op string contains a colon. Core ops — `send`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `voice_self_state`, etc. — contain no colon. The registry uses last-writer-wins with no blocklist of protected names. If a Bootstrap-Admin adds a plugin whose `plugin.toml` declares `ws_ops = ["send"]` and whose `backend` registers a `"send"` handler, the permission-gate check at activation time accepts it (the op is declared), and at dispatch time the gate is skipped (no colon). The rogue handler then runs for every WebSocket user's `send` message with no allowlist, membership, or guild-permission check, bypassing all channel permission enforcement in `ws_op_send.py`.

This requires admin privilege to deploy the plugin, but because the admin UI presents this as a routine "add a plugin" operation with no visible warning about core-op override, a compromised or malicious admin account can silently break the authorization model for all users on the instance.
recommendation: Maintain a frozenset of core (non-namespaced) op names in `ws_ops_registry.py` and reject registration of those names from plugin-loaded modules in `PluginManager.activate()`. The permission gate in `manifest.py` / `permissions.py` should also flag any declared `ws_ops` entry that lacks a colon prefix as a violation in `strict` mode.

verdict.reasoning:
The vulnerability is substantiated by reading the actual code. Three facts from the real source confirm the claim:

1. **Gate condition is colon-gated** (`ws_ops.py` line 119): `if isinstance(op, str) and parse_plugin_op(op) is not None` — `parse_plugin_op` in `ws_op_gate.py` line 158 returns `None` for any string without a colon. A plugin that registers the bare op name `"send"` would match in the dispatch table (`get_handler("send")`) but would then skip the gate block entirely because `parse_plugin_op("send")` is `None`.

2. **Registry is last-writer-wins with no core-op blocklist** (`ws_ops_registry.py` lines 27–30, 97–99): The docstring literally says "Last writer wins. We do not warn on override — that's the contract a plugin needs to override a core op for an A/B experiment." There is no `frozenset` of protected names, no guard in `register_ws_op`, and no check in `PluginManager.activate()` for non-namespaced op names.

3. **Permission gate (Schritt 5) does not enforce colon-namespace on declared ops** (`permissions.py` lines 112–126, `registry.py` lines 170–187): `compute_violations` computes `new_ops - declared_ops`. If `plugin.toml` declares `ws_ops = ["send"]` and the plugin registers `"send"`, the set difference is empty — no violation is flagged. The manifest model (`manifest.py` line 64) stores `ws_ops: list[str]` with no regex constraint requiring a colon.

The exploit path is: admin adds a plugin with `ws_ops = ["send"]` in its `plugin.toml` whose `backend.py` calls `register_ws_op("send", rogue_handler)`. After activation, every WebSocket client message with `op: "send"` dispatches to the rogue handler (line 140 in `ws_ops.py`: `await handler(ctx, msg)`) with no allowlist, membership, or channel-permission check — completely bypassing `ws_op_send.py`.

The severity is appropriately medium (not critical) because it requires a malicious or compromised Bootstrap-Admin account to deploy the plugin, which is already a privileged position. However, the admin UI gives no indication that declaring a core op name in `ws_ops` is semantically different from declaring a namespaced op, making the attack vector non-obvious and the authorization bypass total once triggered.

title: tamagotchi:reset has no guild-admin gate — any member can wipe shared pet state

The plugin's own comment at line 69 acknowledges that a `MANAGE_GUILD` gate was planned for a rename op but was explicitly deferred. The ws_op_gate framework already receives `guild_id` and `user_id`; the tamagotchi handler has access to `ctx.manager._session_factory` and can perform the same `check_permission` call that HTTP routes use.

The `_mutate_reset` function at line 137 ignores the current state and returns a fresh `DEFAULT_STATE` — a full wipe. There is no per-action authorization check and no `MANAGE_GUILD` check anywhere in the `reset` dispatch path. title: Plugin gate error messages disclose instance allowlist contents to any authenticated user
description: The gate returns distinct error codes and human-readable messages depending on why a plugin op was rejected: code 4040 `"plugin not allowed: {plugin_name}"` means the plugin name exists as a string key in `app.state.plugin_allowlist` (or does not); code 4043 `"plugin not enabled for guild: {plugin_name}"` confirms the plugin is in the allowlist. Any authenticated WebSocket user can send arbitrary `{"op": "<name>:ping"}` frames and use the response codes to enumerate exactly which plugins are installed and enabled on the instance, without being a guild member. This leaks the server's plugin configuration to all users.

The `error_msg` string should not embed the plugin name for non-allowlist rejections. Membership-check errors (4042) can safely include the generic message they already have.

The code in ws_op_gate.py (lines 252-283) confirms the distinct error paths: code 4040 "plugin not allowed: {plugin_name}" fires when the plugin is absent from the allowlist, while 4043 "plugin not enabled for guild: {plugin_name}" fires when it IS in the allowlist but not guild-enabled. Both messages also embed the plugin name. The dispatcher in ws_ops.py lines 131-138 passes both `error_code` and `error_msg` directly to the client as JSON.

One nuance the reviewer got slightly wrong: reaching 4043 requires passing the 4042 membership check first (lines 271-276 in ws_op_gate.py), so 4043 is only reachable by actual guild members — not "any authenticated user without guild membership." However, any guild member can trivially distinguish allowlist status by sending a plugin op and observing 4040 vs 4043.

A second partial mitigation the reviewer missed: the handler registry lookup (`get_handler`, ws_ops.py line 108) happens *before* the gate. If the plugin op is not registered in `_handlers`, the response is the generic 4007 "unknown op" and the gate never runs. So enumeration is bounded to ops that are currently loaded and registered — the attacker must know (or guess) a valid registered op name like `tamagotchi:feed`. This means the leak is real but slightly narrower than "enumerate any plugin name," since you must already know the op name to probe with.

For the registered ops that do exist (`tamagotchi:feed/play/sleep/reset`, `hello:ping`), a guild member can determine whether `tamagotchi` is in the instance allowlist vs. only loaded-but-not-allowlisted. The severity is low as stated: it leaks server plugin configuration, not authentication tokens or user data, and requires a valid authenticated WebSocket session plus guild membership to reach 4043.

title: idbPutIdentity resolves on request success instead of transaction commit
description: The `idbPutIdentity` helper resolves the returned Promise on `req.onsuccess` (the IDB request succeeded) rather than on `tx.oncomplete` (the transaction was durably committed to disk). IndexedDB spec guarantees that data is only durably persisted when the transaction's `oncomplete` fires. Between `req.onsuccess` and `tx.oncomplete`, a tab crash or browser kill can silently drop the write. title: Ed25519 private key generated as extractable — XSS can permanently exfiltrate identity credential
description: The Ed25519 private key is unconditionally generated with `extractable: true` (line 89, `generateKey({name:'Ed25519'}, true, ['sign','verify'])`). The stated rationale is Cloud-backup convenience. Because the key is extractable, any script running in the same origin — e.g. via a stored XSS in a chat message, a compromised CDN asset, or a malicious browser extension — can call `window.crypto.subtle.exportKey('pkcs8' | 'raw', privateKey)` and obtain the raw 32-byte secret. This private key is the sole proof-of-possession that authenticates the user on every self-host server via the Cert-Login challenge-response flow (cert-login.ts). A stolen key lets an attacker impersonate the user on any self-host instance indefinitely (cert validity up to ~1 year). Unlike a stolen session token, the attacker can re-run the cert-login challenge at any time without the victim's presence. Non-extractable keys (`extractable: false`) receive no additional hardware isolation in most browsers, but they do prevent JS-level export. The backup flow already has a per-user workaround path (the 'Bitte neu anmelden' fallback), making the always-extractable policy unnecessary for security.
recommendation: Change `generateKey` to use `extractable: false` by default. For the backup flow, prompt the user to export once at backup-creation time (the backup dialog already handles this path) rather than keeping the key permanently exportable. The `forBackup` parameter already exists as a hook; route it to a one-shot export operation rather than storing an always-extractable key.
