The `forBackup` parameter is explicitly voided at line 78 (`void opts;`) with a comment stating it has no effect. The `supportsWebCryptoEd25519()` detection function at line 31 uses `extractable: false`, proving the non-extractable form works fine — the always-extractable decision is a deliberate policy choice. The exploit path is fully reachable: same-origin JS can call `window.crypto.subtle.exportKey('pkcs8'|'raw', privateKey)` to extract the 32-byte Ed25519 secret. The cert-login backend (`cert_login.py`) confirms this private key is the sole proof-of-possession — the verify step checks an Ed25519 signature over a server nonce using `device_pubkey` from the cert, so a stolen key enables indefinite impersonation on any self-host server. The CSP in app.html contains `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'` for `script-src`, meaning it provides no meaningful XSS barrier. Unlike a session token theft, the attacker can re-run the challenge-response at any time with the exfiltrated key and the (also IndexedDB-accessible) cert. Reviewer's recommendation is correct: `extractable: false` at generation time, with a one-shot export only at backup-creation time via the existing backup dialog flow.

title: HTTP self-host server URL accepted and stored without TLS upgrade — session tokens sent in cleartext
description: `normalizeHostname` in `servers.svelte.ts` (line 31-37) accepts URLs that already start with `http://` and returns them unchanged. `server-info.ts:normalizeHostname` (line 47-57) correctly upgrades `http://` to `https://`, but this upgraded value flows into `addServerWithCertLogin` → `serversStore.add(args.hostname, ...)`. The dangerous path is the Electron deep-link invite handler at `web/src/routes/invite/[code]/+page.svelte:24-29`: `deepLinkHostname` is derived from the raw `?host=` URL parameter and accepts `http://` without upgrading (lines 25-27 only prepend `https://` when neither prefix is present). This `http://` hostname is then passed directly to `serversStore.add` (line 46). Any subsequent REST calls to this server go over plaintext HTTP (client.ts:94 uses `server.hostname` verbatim), leaking Bearer session tokens. The WS connection always uses `wss://` (gateway-connection.ts:215-216), but all authenticated REST requests go over cleartext. An attacker who can craft a `pulse://invite?host=http://...` deep link and lure the user into clicking it can intercept session tokens.
recommendation: Enforce HTTPS in `servers.svelte.ts:normalizeHostname`: replace the current `if (!trimmed.startsWith('https://') && !trimmed.startsWith('http://'))` branch with one that also upgrades `http://` to `https://`, matching the logic in `server-info.ts`. Additionally, validate in `+page.svelte` that `deepLinkHostname` starts with `https://` before calling `serversStore.add`.

The vulnerability is partially real but the reviewer's primary attack scenario (Electron deep-link) is mitigated by an existing guard the reviewer missed.

**What the reviewer got right:**
- `servers.svelte.ts:normalizeHostname` (lines 31-37) does accept and store `http://` URLs verbatim — confirmed by reading the code.
- `+page.svelte` lines 25-27 preserve an `http://` prefixed `rawHost` without upgrading it — confirmed.
- `client.ts:buildUrl` (line 94) uses `server.hostname` verbatim: `return \`${server.hostname}${ep}${path}\`` — REST calls to an `http://` hostname would be cleartext.
- WS at `gateway-connection.ts:215-216` always forces `wss://`, so only REST is affected.

**What the reviewer missed — the guard that blocks the Electron path:**
`desktop/electron/main.ts:handleDeepLink` (lines 169-176) extracts the `host` from `pulse://invite?host=<value>` as a bare hostname (no scheme), validates it with `_isValidFqdn()` which uses a regex that only allows `[a-z0-9-]` label characters and dots — this rejects any value containing `://`. Even if someone tried `pulse://invite?host=http://evil.example.com`, the `_isValidFqdn` check at line 173 would reject it (`http://` contains colons and slashes, which fail the regex) and the deep-link is silently dropped. The payload sent to the renderer is the bare FQDN string (no scheme prefix), so `+page.svelte` always hits the `https://${rawHost}` fallback for Electron-originated deep-links.

**What IS exploitable — the browser path:**
A crafted browser URL `https://howispulse.com/invite/CODE?host=http://attacker.example.com` (navigated to directly in a browser, not via Electron deep-link) reaches `+page.svelte` with `rawHost = "http://attacker.example.com"`. The page preserves this as `deepLinkHostname = "http://attacker.example.com"` (lines 25-27). After the user clicks "Weiter", `serversStore.add("http://attacker.example.com")` stores it with `http://`, and subsequent REST calls prepend the `http://` hostname, sending Bearer session tokens over cleartext to the attacker-controlled server. This path requires the attacker to: (a) craft the URL, (b) get the user to click it in a browser, and (c) have the user then click "Weiter" on the disclaimer, and (d) MITM or control the `http://attacker.example.com` server to capture the tokens.

**Adjusted severity:** The Electron deep-link attack (the higher-risk path) is blocked. The browser path is real but requires explicit user interaction through a disclaimer. Severity is medium rather than high.

title: Access and refresh tokens stored in `localStorage` — accessible to same-origin scripts

At minimum, ensure all message content is properly sanitized before rendering to limit XSS exposure.

title: WS authentication token exposed as URL query parameter — appears in server logs and browser history
description: The authentication token is appended as `?token=<value>` to the WebSocket URL (gateway-connection.ts:212 for Cloud, 216 for Self-Host). This is the documented design (CLAUDE.md: 'WS-Auth: Access-Token als Query-Param — Browser-WebSocket-API kann keine Custom-Header'). The impact is that the token appears in: (1) web server / nginx / Caddy access logs in plaintext, (2) browser developer tools network tab URL field, (3) any TLS-terminating proxy or WAF that logs request lines. If logs are stored or monitored by parties other than the instance operator, this constitutes token leakage. For the Cloud instance this is mitigated because TLS is end-to-end and logs are operator-controlled. For self-host instances, this depends on the operator's log configuration.
recommendation: This is a known browser WebSocket limitation. As a mitigation, ensure nginx/Caddy access log configurations on the server side exclude or redact the query string for the `/api/ws/ws` path. Document this for self-host operators. Alternatively, consider a two-step approach: establish WS without auth, then send the token in the first frame (though this introduces a window where unauthenticated connections exist).

title: Bypass screen-share: orphaned LiveKit video publication on audio-publish failure

title: connect(): missing generation re-check after startAudio() allows stale connect to corrupt voiceState and enable mic on the wrong room
description: The generation guard (`gen !== this.#connectGen`) is checked at line 290 and correctly handles the case where the LiveKit handshake was superseded. title: Plugin permission gate can be silently disabled at runtime via globalThis

However, the permission gate is the only software control preventing a plugin from registering undeclared WS op handlers; disabling it allows a rogue plugin to silently escalate its declared capabilities for all plugins loaded after it.

Additionally, set `PULSE_PLUGIN_PERMISSIONS` explicitly in `vite.config.ts` as a `define` constant (e.g., `'import.meta.env.PULSE_PLUGIN_PERMISSIONS': JSON.stringify('strict')`) so Vite inlines it as a dead-code-eliminatable literal and the `globalThis` fallback is never reached in the production bundle.

1. `import.meta.env.PULSE_PLUGIN_PERMISSIONS` is indeed inlined as `void 0` in the compiled output (`settings.svelte.js:5986`) because `vite.config.ts` has no `define` entry for it.

2. The `globalThis` fallback branch IS the actual runtime code path in production - confirmed by inspecting the compiled output.

3. `resolvePluginPermissionMode()` IS called at line 168 of `registry.ts`, AFTER `await register()` at line 160. This means a plugin's `register()` function runs before the permission mode is sampled, so `globalThis.PULSE_PLUGIN_PERMISSIONS = 'off'` set inside `register()` will affect the gate for that same plugin activation. Because `loadAll()` activates plugins sequentially (`for ... await activatePlugin(name)`), the `globalThis` mutation also persists and disables the gate for all subsequently activated plugins.

The soft-sandbox is a defence against *accidental* capability inflation, not malicious plugins." The permission gate is intentionally documented as a hygiene check, not a security boundary. A rogue plugin that can run `register()` code already has unrestricted access to `localStorage` tokens, can call any API endpoint, and can import any `$lib` module directly - it does not need to manipulate `globalThis` to "escalate" anything. The gate's only real purpose is to catch developer mistakes where a plugin registers more than it declared.

The TOCTOU is real and the recommendation (freeze the mode at module load with a top-level `const MODE = resolvePluginPermissionMode()`) is correct and would eliminate the window. title: DriftCorrector: hard-seek applies 1.5s lookahead to paused state, placing viewer 1.5s ahead of host

title: WhepPlayer: `ontrack` fires per-track, calling onTrack twice — video element briefly unmuted before Web Audio graph attaches

title: Image decoded twice per upload: redundant createImageBitmap call in _measureImage

title: Content-Disposition filename injection in presigned GET URLs
description: The `presigned_get_url` function builds the `ResponseContentDisposition` header value by string-interpolating the raw `filename` from the database: `f'attachment; filename="{filename}"'`. The filename field in `AttachmentUploadIn` is validated only for length (1–255 chars) and has no character restrictions. A user can upload a file named `evil"; x-injected: value` — the resulting `Content-Disposition` header emitted by MinIO becomes `attachment; filename="evil"; x-injected: value"`. MinIO is reverse-proxied under the same origin as the application (`howispulse.com/s3/`). While authentication uses `Authorization: Bearer` headers stored in localStorage (not HttpOnly cookies), the injection enables header-smuggling attacks on same-origin MinIO responses: an attacker member can craft a filename that causes MinIO to emit an unexpected `Content-Type` header (e.g. `text/html`) on what is nominally a download, potentially enabling reflected content execution for any user who follows the presigned link.
recommendation: Escape or sanitize the filename before embedding it in the header value. Use RFC 5987 encoding (`filename*=UTF-8''<percent-encoded>`) via Python's `urllib.parse.quote` instead of the bare double-quoted form, or at minimum strip/replace `"` and `\r\n` characters: `filename.replace('"', '').replace('\r', '').replace('\n', '')`. For the presigned URL, pass the parameter as `filename*=UTF-8''<encoded>` which avoids quoting entirely.

verdict.reasoning:
The unescaped filename interpolation is real: `/home/michael/Dokumente/pulse/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/s3.py` line 157–159 does `f'attachment; filename="{filename}"'` with no escaping, and `AttachmentUploadIn.filename` in schemas.py line 185 only validates `min_length=1, max_length=255` — no character restrictions. Pydantic v2 confirmed to pass through `"`, `;`, and CRLF without stripping.

However, the reviewer's stated impact is significantly overstated and partially wrong:

1. The `ResponseContentDisposition` S3 parameter becomes a URL-encoded query parameter in the presigned URL. MinIO decodes it and emits the decoded value as the `Content-Disposition` response header. So a crafted filename like `evil"; x-injected: value` produces a malformed `Content-Disposition` header, not a new `x-injected` header. Semicolons are parameter separators *within* Content-Disposition, not HTTP header line separators.

2. The reviewer's key claim — that injecting `; content-type: text/html` into the Content-Disposition value causes MinIO to emit a different `Content-Type` header — is incorrect. That is not how HTTP header parsing works. You cannot inject new HTTP headers via semicolons in a header value; you need CRLF (`\r\n`).

3. CRLF injection (the only real path to new-header injection) is blocked at the MinIO layer: MinIO is a Go server, and Go's `net/http` package rejects response header values containing `\r\n` (introduced in Go 1.7, enforced strictly in later versions). This makes the CRLF-based `Content-Type` injection path non-exploitable.

4. The injection only triggers at all when `inline=False`, which only applies to non-renderable MIME types (zip, exe, etc. — not image/, video/, audio/, application/pdf). These types are served as `attachment` disposition, meaning browsers download them rather than render them, further limiting any HTML-execution scenario.

The real (confirmed) impact is a malformed `Content-Disposition` header for filenames containing `"` or other special header characters — this could cause download-filename display issues and is a correctness/RFC compliance bug. The XSS/content-execution path described in the finding is not reachable through this specific vector. The severity should be low rather than medium.

title: Watch-party native video URL allows client-side probing of internal network hosts

title: store:set IPC — no key allowlist allows arbitrary key injection into the persistent store
description: The `store:set` IPC handler accepts any key string from the renderer and writes it directly into `pulse-stream.json`. There is no allowlist of valid keys. A compromised renderer (e.g. XSS on the loaded origin, or a `PULSE_URL`-pointed attacker page) can write arbitrary keys, including very long strings or deeply nested values that bloat the store, or can shadow future keys that other store consumers will read. Because `storeGet` returns `data?.[key]` with no validation, a write of `__proto__` or `constructor` as a key name could in principle cause prototype pollution on the in-memory `data` object (though modern JS engines and `JSON.parse` with a plain object literal generally resist this, it is not explicitly guarded against).

title: nginx sends Connection: close to all non-WebSocket upstreams, preventing TCP keepalive

Even though `proxy_http_version 1.1` is set, this header causes uvicorn to close the connection after each response, and nginx discards the upstream socket. title: proxy_read_timeout 3600s applied at server level, inherited by all REST locations

title: MinIO backup staging area uses ephemeral container overlay filesystem, doubling I/O

description: The `chat-gateway` service in the prod compose has no named volume for its `./data/` directory (relative to `/app/services/chat-gateway/`). The VAPID key file defaults to `./data/vapid.json` (`config.py:160`). When `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` and `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` env vars are empty (as in `.env.example:127-128`), the service generates a new keypair on first startup and writes it to `./data/vapid.json`. Watchtower recreates the container on every image update (every push to main), destroying this directory and regenerating the keypair. Every existing browser push subscription becomes invalid because the server-side public key has changed. The service emits a `vapid_auto_generated` warning log when this happens. This is a service-availability issue: push notifications silently stop working after each deploy until users clear and re-subscribe.
recommendation: Add a named volume for the chat-gateway data directory in `infra/prod/docker-compose.yml` (e.g., `pulse_chat_data:/app/services/chat-gateway/data`), or set `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` and `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` to stable operator-generated values in the production `.env` file. The `.env.example` should be updated to include generation instructions similar to the `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` block.

verdict.reasoning:
All parts of the claim are confirmed by reading the actual code:

1. `/infra/prod/docker-compose.yml:233-251` — the `chat-gateway` service mounts only `./secrets:/secrets:ro` and `pulse_guild_icons:/app/services/chat-gateway/uploads`. There is no volume for the data directory. The named volumes at line 387-393 (`pulse_pg`, `pulse_redis`, `pulse_avatars`, `pulse_guild_icons`, `pulse_minio`, `pulse_backups`) confirm no `pulse_chat_data` volume exists.

2. `/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/config.py:160` — `vapid_key_file` defaults to `"./data/vapid.json"`, which is a path inside the container with no persistent backing.

3. `/services/chat-gateway/src/dcc_chat_gateway/vapid.py:110-170` — `ensure_vapid` has a clear fallthrough: if env vars are absent AND the file doesn't exist, it calls `_generate_keypair()` and `_persist_keypair_to_disk()`. The code itself warns at lines 158-168 with the `vapid_auto_generated` log message: "Without persistence (e.g. Docker volume on vapid_key_file path), every restart will invalidate all push subscriptions silently."

4. `/infra/prod/.env.example:122-128` — `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` and `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` are empty by default. The comment explicitly states "NOT persistent across docker restarts without a volume."

5. The compose file's `x-app-labels` enables Watchtower for `chat-gateway`, meaning it is recreated on every image update (every push to main per the comment on line 12-13).

The impact path is real: Watchtower recreates the container → ephemeral `./data/vapid.json` is gone → `ensure_vapid` generates a new keypair → old browser push subscriptions (which embed the old public key) are permanently invalid. The service itself acknowledges this footgun in code comments. The severity is correctly assessed as low (push notifications stop working silently, not a security issue) but the issue is genuine.
